title: Fettuccine Alfredo
subtitle: Roman butter and parmesan pasta
excerpt: The original Roman version of this dish is nothing more than fettuccine tossed with an extravagant amount of butter and freshly grated parmesan until the two form a silky, glossy sauce. No cream. No garlic. No flour. Just three ingredients done correctly.

recipe.sourceNotes: Fettuccine Alfredo was invented around 1914 by Alfredo di Lelio, a restaurateur in Rome, who made it for his wife recovering from childbirth. He enriched a simple buttered pasta with extra butter and parmesan, tossed at the table with golden cutlery. American tourists including Mary Pickford and Douglas Fairbanks encountered the dish in Rome in 1920 and helped make it famous in the United States. The American version evolved to include cream and garlic, but the original Roman dish uses only butter, parmesan, and pasta water.

content.text: The sauce forms from the emulsion of butter, parmesan, and starchy pasta cooking water. The pasta water is not an afterthought: it is the mechanism that allows the butter and cheese to form a sauce rather than two separate ingredients. Use very finely grated parmesan and add it off the direct heat, tossing constantly, or it will clump. The butter should be cold when it goes in.
Cook the fettuccine in a large pan of heavily salted boiling water until al dente. Reserve 300 ml of pasta water before draining.

Put a wide frying pan or the pasta pot over low heat. Add 150 ml of the pasta water and let it simmer briefly. Add the cold butter piece by piece, moving the pan in a circular motion to emulsify. When the butter is incorporated and the liquid looks creamy, add the drained pasta.

Remove from direct heat. Add three-quarters of the parmesan and toss vigorously, adding more pasta water a tablespoon at a time to keep the sauce fluid. The pasta should be coated in a glossy, clinging sauce. Add remaining parmesan and toss again.
Season with pepper and serve immediately. The sauce thickens fast: it must be served the moment it is ready.
